findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement of £386m substantially exceeds borrowing of £289m, with £97m gap filled by reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The council's underlying need to borrow (CFR) is £386m, but external borrowing stands at only £288.977m. The £97m gap is being bridged by re-investing internal reserves and cash balances, which yields lower returns than debt costs but depletes the council's financial buffer.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund capital rather than borrowing erodes the council's reserves and flexibility. Once reserves are exhausted, the council will need to borrow further or defer capital spending.
findings.figures: CFR £386m; borrowing £288.977m; reserve funding gap £97m
findings.quote: The difference between the CFR of £386m and the Borrowing Portfolio of £288.977m represents re-investment of the internal balances including reserves, reducing the in-year borrowing costs in excess of the potential investment returns.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Pension contribution prepayment consumed £20m of annual new borrowing
findings.detail: Of the £90m in new borrowing taken during the year, £20m was specifically drawn to fund an annual pension contribution prepayment. The remaining £70m replaced maturing loans. This represents a deliberate commitment to advance pension funding.
findings.matters: Pension prepayment decisions indicate forward cash planning but also represent a committed outflow that reduces borrowing capacity available for other capital or service needs.
findings.figures: £20m for pension prepayment; £70m to replace maturing debt; total new borrowing £90m
findings.quote: £20.000m of new loans taken out to cover the annual pension contribution prepayment and to maintain the Council's liquidity indicator above £15.000m

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital programme rephasing reduced debt repayment charges in the year
findings.detail: The council achieved a £2.087m underspend on interest and capital financing costs, with the Minimum Revenue Provision charge £0.181m below budget. This was attributable to delays in capital project delivery, signalling the council is not spending capital at the pace originally planned.
findings.matters: Capital programme delays indicate delivery risk and suggest planned capital spending may not materialise, which affects medium-term financial planning and service infrastructure investment.
findings.figures: MRP underspend £0.181m; total interest & capital financing variance £2.087m under budget
findings.quote: a lower Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) charge, reflecting the rephasing of capital projects

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Strategic investment portfolio showing £2.3m unrealised loss against purchase cost
findings.detail: The council holds £10m in strategic pooled funds now valued at £7.704m as at 31 March 2026. The CCLA property fund has fallen to £4.253m from £5m cost; FP Foresight infrastructure fund to £2.146m from £3m; VT Gravis clean energy fund to £1.304m from £2m. Losses are currently shielded from the revenue account by statutory override, but protection expires in 2029/30, at which point the council faces potential charges to revenue.
findings.matters: 23% capital loss on strategic holdings represents a deferred revenue pressure when the statutory override expires in 2029/30, or if the council needs to realise these investments earlier. This erodes financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Historic cost £10m; fair value £7.704m; CCLA £4.253m on £5m cost; Infrastructure fund £2.146m on £3m; Clean energy £1.304m on £2m
findings.quote: In the current economic environment of high interest rates, weak growth, rising inflation and global uncertainty, the value of equity, bonds and property have fallen significantly since the time of investment.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring, Cash Limits and Virements – 202627 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Heritage Services income under pressure from geopolitical factors, already £0.123m behind budget at May
findings.detail: Heritage Services (Roman Baths) achieved a net surplus of £11.738m in 2025/26 but fell £2.545m short of its rebased target due to lower visitor numbers. At end May 2026, admission income is already £0.123m (2.6%) behind budget. Geopolitical instability affecting Middle East transit, US inflation reducing visitor flows, and Asia-Pacific travel disruption are identified as material risks to forecast visitor numbers.
findings.matters: Heritage is a major revenue source (£11.7m+ net) but is highly exposed to external macro factors (geopolitics, currency, fuel costs) outside management control. The May shortfall suggests the risk is materialising early in the year. Q1 forecast is already showing real variance.
findings.figures: £11.738m net surplus 2025/26, £2.545m below target 2025/26, £0.123m (2.6%) behind budget May 2026, £0.000m-£0.750m forecast risk range
findings.quote: Heritage income figures are highly depended on tourist visitor numbers to the Roman Baths. With geo-political instability affecting inbound visitation, in particular from the US, due to inflation, and from Asia-Pacific, due to percentage of visitors who transit through Dubai / Doha, there is considerable risk to the budgeted visitor numbers for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring, Cash Limits and Virements – 202627 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Home to School Transport statutory service overspend recurring: £0.769m adverse in 2025/26, £0.4m-£0.8m risk in 2026/27
findings.detail: This statutory service overran by £0.769m in 2025/26 despite the budget being grown by £0.336m for inflation. Q1 forecasts continued risk of £0.4m-£0.8m as operator costs rise faster than assumed inflation and demand continues to grow. The council cannot refuse provision of this service but cannot control demand.
findings.matters: This is a statutory obligation with uncontrolled demand and supplier costs outpacing budget assumptions. The service is demonstrating a structural cost growth trend. The council must either find further budget or cut provision (not an option), making this a committed future pressure.
findings.figures: £0.769m adverse 2025/26 outturn, £0.336m inflation growth in 2026/27 budget, £0.400m-£0.800m forecast risk 2026/27
findings.quote: Home to School Transport ended 2025/26 with a £0.769m adverse outturn position... The need to respond to continued increases in demand for Home to School Transport, alongside operator cost pressures exceeding assumed inflation, presents an ongoing risk to the budgetary position currently estimated between £0.400m and £0.800m.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring, Cash Limits and Virements – 202627 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit reached £46.505m, additional overspend anticipated for 2026/27, funding dependent on DfE SEND plan approval
findings.detail: DSG overspent by £13.716m in 2025/26, taking the cumulative deficit to £46.505m (ringfenced from general fund but material governance issue). Additional overspend for 2026/27 is anticipated driven by SEND costs. The council submitted its SEND Reform Plan to the DfE on 19 June 2026 (deadline date) and is awaiting approval for the High Needs Stability Grant, which would provide mitigation.
findings.matters: While ringfenced, a £46.5m cumulative deficit is material and growing. The SEND overspend is driving this growth. Funding mitigation depends on external approval that is not yet secured. The council has no control over the approval timeline or outcome.
findings.figures: £13.716m overspend 2025/26, £46.505m cumulative deficit at 31/03/2026, SEND Reform Plan submitted 19 June 2026
findings.quote: The Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) overspent by £13.716m for 2025/26 taking the cumulative to deficit at the end of 2025/26 to £46.505m... Additional overspend for 2026/27 is anticipated at a higher level.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring, Cash Limits and Virements – 202627 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Commercial Income Risk Reserve being rapidly depleted from £3.94m to £0.84m, limiting buffer for income volatility
findings.detail: The reserve created to weather commercial income fluctuations is being drawn down by £2.4m to mitigate pressures in Commercial Estate, Bath Quays South, and the Housing Delivery Company (Aequus). This reduces the reserve from £3.942m to £0.840m, leaving minimal headroom. Further income deterioration would rapidly exhaust this buffer.
findings.matters: Reserves are the council's shock absorber for income volatility. A buffer of £0.84m on a £117m capital programme and council-wide commercial operations is minimal. Depletion signals the council is moving into a less defensible financial position.
findings.figures: Opening balance £3.942m, planned draw £2.400m, residual balance £0.840m
findings.quote: The available balance on the reserve brought forward from 2025/26 is £3.942m. The Quarter 1 forecast assumes that £2.400m of this reserve will be required to mitigate against the overall forecast position, based on taking the mid-point range of risk forecast for those income streams reported above, which would reduce this reserve to £0.840m.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring, Cash Limits and Virements – 202627 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Commercial asset portfolio materially underperforming: Bath Quays South and Commercial Estate combining for £1.1m-£1.65m forecast risk
findings.detail: Bath Quays South offices were £0.665m adverse in 2025/26; Commercial Estate was £0.511m adverse. Both are forecast to continue underperforming in 2026/27 with combined risk of £1.1m-£1.65m. Rental income shortfalls are the key driver, with properties held void while being marketed. The council is also paying increased borrowing costs to support these underperforming assets.
findings.matters: These are balance-sheet assets supposed to generate council revenue. Persistent underperformance raises concerns about asset quality, management effectiveness, and the affordability of the borrowing that finances them. The void holdings also represent stranded capital.
findings.figures: £0.665m Bath Quays adverse 2025/26, £0.511m Commercial Estate adverse 2025/26, £1.100m-£1.650m combined forecast risk
findings.quote: The Commercial Estate ended 2025/26 £0.511m over budget and this adverse position is currently considered likely to continue into 2026/27. The Bath Quays South Office rental income target...ended 2025/26 with an adverse budget position of £0.665m... the current forecast is a material budget pressure of £1.100m - £1.650m.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring, Cash Limits and Virements – 202627 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Children's Services structural overspend recurring: £10.2m actual loss in 2025/26, £5.4m-£8.9m forecast for 2026/27
findings.detail: Children's Services overran by £10.182m in 2025/26 driven by residential placement demand and care cost pressures. Q1 2026/27 forecasts another £5.35m-£8.9m overspend despite growth allocation and a focused transformation programme. The council has established a placements taskforce and is engaging with regional networks, but uncontrolled demand continues to outpace budget.
findings.matters: This is the single largest identified budget risk and is recurring across consecutive years. It represents uncontrolled demand pressure in a statutory service directly affecting council financial standing. Even the best-case forecast (£5.35m) is material.
findings.figures: £10.182m overspend 2025/26, £5.350m-£8.900m forecast 2026/27, residential placements 155 (May 2026) vs 143 (May 2025)
findings.quote: Children's Services closed the 2025/26 financial year with a £10.182m overspend, largely driven by continued demand and residential placement costs... a significant material forecast of £5.350m - £8.900m over budget is currently being projected.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budget Monitoring, Cash Limits and Virements – 202627 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Council forecasts £5.32m Q1 adverse variance, requiring full contingency and reserve depletion
findings.detail: The Q1 forecast shows an adverse net variance of £5.32m, mitigated by using the full £2.68m corporate contingency and a £2.4m draw from the Commercial Income Risk Reserve. Directorates have been tasked with developing recovery plans by Q2, but the underlying risk across the organisation remains high. This leaves minimal headroom for further pressures.
findings.matters: The council is relying on full use of contingency at Q1, when typically headroom should extend further into the year. If recovery plans don't materialise and reserves are depleted, the council loses financial flexibility and may struggle to absorb unexpected pressures.
findings.figures: £5.320m adverse variance, £2.680m corporate contingency (fully used), £2.400m Commercial Income Risk Reserve draw
findings.quote: The forecast position of the Council's 2026/27 Revenue Budget as at the end of Quarter 1 (June 2026) is an adverse net variance of £5.320m mitigated by Corporate Contingency Release & Commercial Income Risk Reserve Utilisation.

findings.paper_title: E3653 Appendix 5 - Revenue Savings Monitor
findings.headline: Regeneration services unable to achieve savings targets due to grant income dependency and cost recovery constraints
findings.detail: The Regeneration service reports that both new and existing savings targets are challenging to meet because the service is heavily dependent on grant income already bid for and has very limited ability to recover additional costs elsewhere.
findings.matters: When services depend on external grant funding to meet savings targets, the council loses control over achieving its budget plan if grants are not awarded or are withdrawn; this signals structural vulnerability in budget delivery
findings.figures: £50k variance on new regeneration income (partially mitigated by one-off income)
findings.quote: Both new and historic savings targets are challenging to meet. The service is highly dependant upon grant income which has already been bid for with very limited opportunities to recover extra costs.

findings.paper_title: E3653 Appendix 5 - Revenue Savings Monitor
findings.headline: Multiple property and commercial income targets not materialising; three separate delays totalling £625k
findings.detail: Commercial property income is £200k short due to underperformance between commercial and corporate portfolios. Corporate Estate disposal savings of £275k have not materialised because identified properties have minimal impact on running costs. Bath Quays South office building has £150k delayed income target due to partial vacancy; full occupancy not expected until May 2026.
findings.matters: Persistent property and commercial income shortfalls across multiple parts of the portfolio suggest the council's asset strategy is not generating expected returns, indicating either occupancy challenges or slower lease-up than planned
findings.figures: Commercial Estate £200k shortfall; Corporate Estate £275k delay; Bath Quays South £150k delay
findings.quote: A shortfall in income target between the Commercial and Corporate Estates has led to a delay in achieving this savings target.

findings.paper_title: E3653 Appendix 5 - Revenue Savings Monitor
findings.headline: Roman Baths visitor income continues below budget; £2.454m adverse variance in 2025/26, rebased for 2026/27
findings.detail: Visitor numbers to the Roman Baths remain below the 1.1m budgeted target, preventing the service from achieving its budgeted surplus. The 2025/26 outturn shows an adverse variance of £2.454m. The council has rebased 2026/27 income targets downward in a revised business plan, treating this as permanent income loss rather than temporary underperformance.
findings.matters: Structural erosion of income from a major council asset suggests either the visitor market has changed or the original business case was optimistic; the council is now absorbing this as ongoing budget pressure
findings.figures: £2.454m adverse outturn 2025/26; 1.1m visitor target; £2.148m ongoing budget pressure
findings.quote: As a result of a continuation of visitor numbers below the budgeted 1.1m at the Roman Baths, the Service has not achieved the budgeted surplus. The 25/26 Outturn position is an adverse £2.454m.

findings.paper_title: E3653 Appendix 5 - Revenue Savings Monitor
findings.headline: £2m staffing restructuring saving from Being Our Best programme not delivered; execution delayed
findings.detail: The council budgeted for £2.5m of staffing savings from the Being Our Best organisational restructuring in 2024/25 plus a further £2m in 2025/26. Delays to the programme mean it will only partially deliver, with the full £2m 2025/26 savings now not achieved. This cascades into delays to service restructuring proposals.
findings.matters: A major staffing restructuring falling short by £2m signals execution risk on a core efficiency plan the council built its budget around; this represents ongoing structural cost pressure that will need to be addressed
findings.figures: £2m variance; £2.5m 2024/25 target plus £2m 2025/26 target
findings.quote: The programme will partially deliver against the £2.5m built into the budget for 2024/25, but will not deliver the additional £2m in the 2025/26 budget

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Cabinet Report 25-26
findings.headline: Collection Fund adverse variance of £0.240m worse than estimated; Council Tax deficit of £0.562m created unexpected pressure
findings.detail: The outturn Collection Fund position was £0.240m worse than the provision made in the 2026/27 budget. Council Tax in particular was adversely affected by lower second homes and long-term empty properties, student occupied property increases, and bad debt write-offs, creating a £0.562m deficit of which the council's share was £0.218m. The total council share of the Collection Fund deficit increased by £0.396m from budget estimate.
findings.matters: Income forecasting accuracy is deteriorating, and the council is facing recurring council tax collection issues (bad debt, property classification changes) that suggest underlying collection risk.
findings.figures: £0.240m total variance worse than estimated; £0.562m Council Tax deficit; £0.218m council share; £0.396m worse than budget estimate; £1.724m Business Rates deficit (council share)
findings.quote: The non LCTS elements of the Collection Fund ended the year in an adverse position, with a deficit of £0.935m mainly due to less than budgeted second homes and long-term empty properties where a premium is charged, an increase in student occupied properties and a higher than forecast increase in the bad debt provision.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Cabinet Report 25-26
findings.headline: General Fund un-earmarked reserve sits at £12.584m, within but tight to the £12.0m–£13.2m risk range
findings.detail: The uncommitted non-earmarked reserve of £12.584m is within the budget risk assessment range set for 2026/27 (£12.0m–£13.2m), but there is minimal headroom. Further deterioration would breach the lower bound and require reserves to be rebuilt in future years.
findings.matters: The council has limited headroom for unforeseen shocks or if the structural pressures (children's services, SEND) continue to worsen. Any further reserve drawdown would leave the council below its minimum comfort level.
findings.figures: £12.584m actual; £12.0m–£13.2m target range
findings.quote: The year-end position of uncommitted non-earmarked reserves was £12.584m. The 2026/27 budget risk assessment, contained within the Budget and Council Tax 2026/27 and Financial Outlook Report to Council on 24th February 2026 set a range of between £12.0m and £13.2m to meet those risks.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Cabinet Report 25-26
findings.headline: Home to School Transport continues to pressure budget with rising SEN demand costs
findings.detail: Home to School Transport presented a £0.769m adverse variance in 2025/26 driven by increased demand, particularly increased Special Educational Needs (SEN) demand. This follows the broader pattern of SEND cost inflation across the council and suggests ongoing structural pressure in this service.
findings.matters: SEN-related cost pressures are appearing across multiple budget lines (residential placements, SEND transport, education staffing), indicating a systemic driver rather than isolated variances.
findings.figures: £0.769m adverse variance; driven by SEN demand increases
findings.quote: Home to School Transport continues to present financial pressure with increased demand, and in particular, increased Special Educational Needs (SEN) demand, resulting in an adverse variance for the service of £0.769m.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Cabinet Report 25-26
findings.headline: Commercial income underperformance: Heritage Services visitor numbers fell short of aggressive budget; Bath Quays South rental delays persist
findings.detail: Heritage Services set an aggressive income target for 2025/26 but visitor numbers fell below budget, particularly during peak pricing periods, creating a £2.454m adverse variance. Combined with one-off restructuring costs, the service outturn was significantly adverse. Bath Quays South floor space rental was delayed, and delays in implementing the corporate landlord model and estate rationalisation contributed a £1.593m variance across Commercial Estate and Regeneration.
findings.matters: Income from heritage and commercial property is not materialising as forecast, suggesting either the budget assumptions were unrealistic or demand drivers have shifted. The ongoing delays in Bath Quays South suggest these are not one-off issues.
findings.figures: £2.454m Heritage Services adverse variance; £1.593m Commercial Estate/Regeneration variance from Bath Quays South delays
findings.quote: An aggressive income target was set for Heritage Services for 2025/26, but unfortunately visitor numbers were lower than budgeted, with larger visitor shortfalls crucially happening during months with peak pricing periods.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Cabinet Report 25-26
findings.headline: Revenue Budget Contingency Reserve drawn by £1.455m; Commercial Income Risk Reserve drawn by £1.176m to cover the outturn
findings.detail: The £2.631m revenue overspend is entirely funded by earmarked reserves rather than managed within budget. The Revenue Budget Contingency was drawn by £1.455m (of which £0.840m was one-off invoices written off), and the Commercial Income Risk Reserve by £1.176m for Commercial Estate (£0.511m) and Bath Quays South (£0.665m) rental income shortfalls. The Commercial Income Risk Reserve was itself created only recently by repurposing reserves and transferring £3.500m from the Business Rates Reserve.
findings.matters: The council is funding operational overspends from reserves created for risk mitigation, not from operational income. This is unsustainable if the underlying drivers (demand, income shortfalls) are structural rather than cyclical.
findings.figures: £2.631m overall revenue overspend; £1.455m from Revenue Budget Contingency; £1.176m from Commercial Income Risk Reserve; Commercial Estate pressure £0.511m; Bath Quays South pressure £0.665m
findings.quote: It is proposed that the £2.631m adverse variance is funded by the following drawdowns from Earmarked Reserves: £1.176m from the Commercial Income Risk Reserve to fund the associated adverse variances within Commercial Estate (£0.511m) and Regeneration (£0.665m).

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Cabinet Report 25-26
findings.headline: Being Our Best Programme delivered only 65% of £14.012m savings target; £2.479m undelivered in-year
findings.detail: Of approved savings proposals totalling £14.012m, 65% (£9.149m) were delivered in full, 15% (£2.040m) were mitigated through contingency elsewhere, and 20% (£2.823m) were delayed into 2026/27. The Pay & Grading Review resulted in a net increase in salary costs of £1.721m, exceeding budget and creating both an in-year and ongoing pressure. The residual £2.209m savings target was carried forward into 2026/27.
findings.matters: Savings programmes are not delivering as planned, and compensation from elsewhere masks underperformance. A pay award has added £1.721m recurring pressure with no offsetting efficiency gain, eroding the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £14.012m total savings target; £9.149m (65%) delivered; £2.823m (20%) delayed; £2.479m in-year shortfall; £2.209m carried forward to 2026/27; £1.721m Pay & Grading overspend
findings.quote: The Savings target relating to the Being our Best Programme in 2025/26 of £2.479m has not been delivered in year.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Cabinet Report 25-26
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant accumulated deficit of £46.505m, with £13.716m added in-year from SEND cost inflation
findings.detail: The centrally held DSG elements overspent by £13.716m due to significant increases in numbers and cost of SEND placements, carried forward with a brought-forward deficit of £32.789m. While the government will provide a High Needs Stability Grant of £41.931m, the council will face a residual £4.573m gap from 2028/29 when the statutory override ends. The DFE has recognised councils will continue to generate deficits until it takes over the High Needs Block in April 2028.
findings.matters: SEND cost inflation is outpacing funding growth. Although ringfenced from the general fund, it signals acute market pressures (placement sufficiency, care complexity, staff inflation) that are hitting the council's controllable services simultaneously.
findings.figures: £46.505m total DSG overspend; £13.716m in-year addition; £32.789m brought forward; £41.931m High Needs Stability Grant; £4.573m residual gap from 2028/29
findings.quote: The centrally held elements of the DSG were over budget by £13.716m, due to significant increases in numbers and cost of placements for children with SEND, which is funded from the High Needs Block within the DSG.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Outturn Cabinet Report 25-26
findings.headline: Children's Services overspent by £10.182m driven by a structural residential placements crisis
findings.detail: The council closed 2024/25 with a £4.775m overspend in children's services, and despite additional budget provision in 2025/26, the situation worsened. Eight residential placements added in Q4 2024/25 created a recurring £2.700m pressure, compounded by a further £4.567m from additional placements in 2025/26. Of the £8.107m total residential placements overspend, £1.510m arose in Q4 alone, driven by escalation from lower-cost support and the increasing complexity of need requiring higher-cost packages.
findings.matters: This represents a structural demand crisis that is growing year-on-year. The recurring nature of Q4 placement increases and the market-driven cost inflation indicate this is unlikely to be a one-off issue, and the council's own transformation programme may not resolve it at the pace overspending is occurring.
findings.figures: £10.182m overspend; £8.107m residential placements pressure; £4.567m additional placements in 2025/26; £1.510m Q4 2025/26 placements; £2.700m recurring from Q4 2024/25 placements
findings.quote: Of the total residential placements pressure of £8.107m, £1.510m arose in quarter 4 of 2025/26 due to additional placements and revised care planning assumptions.

findings.paper_title: Budget & Council Tax 2026-27 and Financial Outlook
findings.headline: Un-earmarked reserves are at lower end of risk-assessed range (£12.58m vs required £12.0-13.2m), providing limited headroom for unforeseen events
findings.detail: The council's General Fund un-earmarked reserve of £12.58m sits within the risk-assessed range of £12.0-13.2m but represents only 6.5% of Net Budget Requirement. The S151 Officer judges this 'adequate', but it provides minimal buffer. Given the £1.66m Q3 overspend forecast and £2.62m contingency held within the budget, the reserve is constrained.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand financial resilience. Lower reserves reduce flexibility to handle unexpected shocks, economic downturns, or service demand spikes. The council is operating at the minimum safe level.
findings.figures: Un-earmarked reserves £12.58m; risk-assessed range £12.0-13.2m; represents 6.5% of Net Budget Requirement (£193.17m)
findings.quote: The budget risk assessment has set a range of between £12.0m and £13.2m to meet those risks. The available balance is £12.58m which is within the budget risk assessment range and represents 6.5% of the Net Budget Requirement. I consider this to be an adequate working balance.

findings.paper_title: Budget & Council Tax 2026-27 and Financial Outlook
findings.headline: Business Rates reset in 2026/27 introduces significant volatility: baseline redistribution and safety net at 100% indicates high risk exposure
findings.detail: The 2026/27 Business Rates reset redistributes all growth since 2013 based on new needs assessments. The council's retained business rate income is projected at £56.95m with a safety net payment of £0.29m to bring it to baseline of £57.24m. The government has increased the safety net to 100% of baseline for 2026/27 'due to the significant system changes', which implicitly signals the vulnerability of councils in this reset. The council must also manage changes to property valuations, transitional relief scheme, and new multipliers for retail/hospitality.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess income stability. Heavy reliance on safety net payments suggests underlying business rates are weak. Business rate income is volatile and difficult to forecast, particularly in economically sensitive areas.
findings.figures: Retained business rate income projection £56.95m; safety net payment £0.29m; baseline funding level £57.24m; safety net at 100% protection for 2026/27
findings.quote: Due to the significant system changes and the resetting of the Business Rate Retention Scheme in 2026/27, the government has increased the level at which a safety net payment is triggered to 100% of each Council's Baseline Funding Level for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Budget & Council Tax 2026-27 and Financial Outlook
findings.headline: 2025/26 year currently forecast £1.66m over budget, with Children's Services, Adult Services, and Corporate Estate as primary drivers of overspend
findings.detail: As of Q3 2025/26 (mid-year), the council is forecasting a £1.66m overspend, an improvement from £2.42m at Q2. However, this is after using £9.83m of budgeted contingencies and £1.72m from the Job Evaluation and Pay Structure reserve. Children's Services are 'forecasting the largest cost pressure, primarily due to high-cost packages'. The council is managing this year but at the cost of deploying reserves.
findings.matters: A lender needs to monitor whether the council is managing its current year position through genuine cost control or reserve drawdown. Heavy contingency use in the current year signals pressures are larger than budgeted
findings.figures: 2025/26 forecast over budget £1.66m (Q3); contingencies used £9.83m; Job Evaluation and Pay Structure reserve used £1.72m
findings.quote: The Council is currently forecasting an over budget position at Quarter 3 of £1.66m, which is an improvement of £0.76m from the Quarter 2 position...The £1.66m forecast over budget position includes the use of £9.83m budgeted contingencies and use of the Job Evaluation and Pay Structure reserve (£1.72m).

findings.paper_title: Budget & Council Tax 2026-27 and Financial Outlook
findings.headline: Capital programme increasingly reliant on borrowing: £301.57m of £504.87m (60%) funding over five years is new borrowing, with interest costs rising as a proportion of revenue budget
findings.detail: The capital programme for 2026-31 totals £504.87m, of which £301.57m (60%) is funded by borrowing. Interest payable as a ratio of net revenue expenditure has risen to 6.33% (2024/25) from 4.90% (2023/24). The CIPFA Financial Resilience Index flags this as a medium risk. The prudential indicator shows capital financing as 14.86% of net revenue stream in 2026/27, forecast to rise to 17.36% by 2028/29.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess debt sustainability. Rising interest costs combined with constrained revenue budgets reduce financial flexibility and increase vulnerability to interest rate shocks
findings.figures: Borrowing £301.57m of £504.87m total capital financing; Interest payable ratio 6.33% (2024/25, up from 4.90%); Capital financing as % of net revenue stream 14.86% (2026/27) rising to 17.36% (2028/29)
findings.quote: The most significant risk highlighted within the index for the Council is Ratio of Interest Payable and Net Revenue Expenditure. This indicator value is 6.33% for 2024/25, which has increased from 4.90% for 2023/24 and reflects the increase in the reliance of external borrowing

findings.paper_title: Budget & Council Tax 2026-27 and Financial Outlook
findings.headline: Savings delivery track record shows material slippage: only 65% of 2025/26 £14.01m savings target forecast to be delivered in full, with 20% delayed to 2026/27
findings.detail: The council required £14.01m of savings in 2025/26. The paper forecasts 65% (£9.15m) will be delivered in full, 15% (£2.04m) will be mitigated through other savings, and 20% (£2.82m) is delayed until 2026/27 or addressed through budget setting. This slippage pattern creates a rolling forward of unfunded pressures. For 2026/27, £7.24m of new savings are required.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess confidence in the council's ability to deliver planned savings. A 20% slippage rate on structural savings is material and suggests savings plans may be optimistic
findings.figures: 2025/26 savings requirement £14.01m: 65% (£9.15m) forecast delivered in full, 15% (£2.04m) mitigated elsewhere, 20% (£2.82m) delayed to 2026/27
findings.quote: The Council has a good track record in savings delivery, in 2025/26 the budget had a savings requirement of £14.01m, of which 65% (£9.15m) are forecast to be delivered in full, 15% (£2.04m) forecast to be mitigated through savings, contingency or income elsewhere in the respective service, with the remaining 20% (£2.82m) delayed until 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Budget & Council Tax 2026-27 and Financial Outlook
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit of £46.57m by March 2026 with contingent liability on the 10% not covered by government stability grant
findings.detail: The council has an accumulated DSG deficit of £46.574m forecast for 2025/26, primarily from SEND high-needs placements. The government's High Needs Stability Grant covers 90% of historic deficits, but this is conditional on DFE approval of a Local SEND Reform Plan. Critically, the government has stated support 'will not be unlimited'. A renewed plan was submitted in August 2025 awaiting DFE decision. The remaining 10% and any new deficits in 2026/27 and 2027/28 create unfunded liabilities before funding responsibility transfers to the DFE in 2028/29.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand contingent liabilities and whether the council's financial position depends on government decisions outside its control. The 10% uncovered deficit and future year accumulation is a material risk to reserves.
findings.figures: DSG deficit 2024/25 £32.795m carried forward; forecast 2025/26 £46.574m; DFE payments received to date £8.1m of £19.2m agreed; High Needs Stability Grant covers 90%
findings.quote: The Government will make available a High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of historic deficits accrued up to the end of 2025/26 to all local authorities with SEND deficits...the Government will continue to take an appropriate and proportionate approach, though it will not be unlimited.

findings.paper_title: Budget & Council Tax 2026-27 and Financial Outlook
findings.headline: Fair Funding Reform has made Bath & North East Somerset a net loser, with government funding excluding Council Tax falling 15.8% over three years
findings.detail: The council is the fourth lowest funded unitary authority. Core Spending Power grows 8.4% (2026-29) against 15.5% for England. When excluding the council's own Council Tax, government funding falls from £69.2m to £58.26m—a 15.8% reduction. This forces increasing reliance on Council Tax and reduces financial flexibility.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess the council's exposure to government policy changes and whether local tax base can sustain service delivery as central funding declines
findings.figures: Core Spending Power growth 8.4% vs England 15.5%; CSP excluding Council Tax: 2025/26 £69.20m to 2028/29 £58.26m (decline of £10.94m, -15.8%)
findings.quote: For England, CSP for local government is increasing by 15.5% across the three year period covering 2026/27 to 2028/29. For the Council, the CSP is shown to increase by 8.4%, well below the England average and reflecting the negative impact of the Fair Funding changes.

findings.paper_title: Budget & Council Tax 2026-27 and Financial Outlook
findings.headline: Substantial unfunded budget gap from 2027/28 onwards totalling £32.92m over four years
findings.detail: The council achieves a balanced 2026/27 budget but faces a forecast gap of £12.59m in 2027/28, £10.47m in 2028/29, and further gaps in subsequent years. The paper states savings proposals of £7.24m close the 2026/27 gap, but shows 'Remaining Funding Gap' of £32.92m from 2027/28 to 2030/31. This reflects structural mismatch between rising service demand and constrained funding.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's medium-term solvency and whether it can fund rising social care and children's services demand without depleting reserves or requiring exceptional government support
findings.figures: 2027/28 gap £12.59m, 2028/29 gap £10.47m, 2029/30 gap £4.95m, 2030/31 gap £4.91m; total remaining funding gap £32.92m
findings.quote: This illustrates a balanced budget for 2026/27 with a forecast budget gap of £32.92m from 2027/28 to 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: Annex 6 - Capital and Investment Strategy
findings.headline: Adult and children's social care dependent on commercial property returns for funding
findings.detail: Investment property net income of £12.060m (2026/27 forecast) and growing service loan returns directly fund frontline social care services. This creates vulnerability: if property income declines, service provision is at risk unless reserves cover the gap.
findings.matters: Linking statutory service funding to volatile property market returns creates hidden financial risk; a market downturn could force service cuts or additional borrowing.
findings.figures: Net investment property income: £12.060m (2026/27); Net service loan income: £0.825m (2026/27) growing to £4.243m (2028/29)
findings.quote: The revenue income supports Council frontline services including Adult and Children's Social Care Services.

findings.paper_title: Annex 6 - Capital and Investment Strategy
findings.headline: Capital expenditure cliff: programme drops 90% from £210.6m to £20.2m by 2030/31
findings.detail: Capital spending projected to fall from £210.599m (2026/27) to £142.188m (2027/28), £96.846m (2028/29), then sharply to £35.068m (2029/30) and £20.167m (2030/31). The sharp cliff suggests major multi-year schemes ending or new capital constraints emerging.
findings.matters: A sudden drop in capital activity signals either scheme completion or affordability constraints; lenders need clarity on whether this reflects planning or financial stress.

findings.paper_title: Annex 6 - Capital and Investment Strategy
findings.headline: Debt financing costs rising to 17.41% of net revenue by 2028/29 from 14.53% baseline
findings.detail: Combined interest and MRP costs are forecast to increase from 14.53% of net revenue expenditure (2024/25 actual) to 17.41% by 2028/29. Interest payments alone rise from 6.80% to 9.81% over the same period, driven by higher borrowing levels.
findings.matters: Escalating debt service crowds out spending on frontline services; the trajectory suggests affordability pressures emerging in the medium term.
findings.figures: Debt Financing costs: 14.53% (2024/25) → 17.41% (2028/29); Interest payments: 6.80% → 9.81%
findings.quote: Debt Financing costs (interest & MRP) to net revenue expenditure | 14.53% | 14.91% | 12.74% | 14.91% | 17.41%

findings.paper_title: Annex 6 - Capital and Investment Strategy
findings.headline: Council using £87m+ of internal cash reserves instead of market borrowing to avoid high interest costs
findings.detail: The Loans CFR (underlying borrowing need) stands at £372.627m, but actual long-term borrowing is only £285.250m. The council is temporarily closing this gap with internal cash reserves, a strategy that cannot sustain indefinitely as reserves are finite.
findings.matters: Once cash reserves deplete, the council will need to borrow at market rates; lenders need to understand when that inflection point arrives and what it means for future borrowing costs.
findings.figures: Loans CFR: £372.627m; Actual long-term borrowing: £285.250m; Implied internal borrowing: £87.377m
findings.quote: The Council is continuing with an agreed strategy of utilising its cash balances rather than incurring the higher cost of long-term borrowing at present. The strategy can be demonstrated through the Loans CFR at the end of 2024/25 which was £372.627m which outlines the Council's underlying need to borrow compared to the current actual long-term borrowing of £285.250m

findings.paper_title: Annex 6 - Capital and Investment Strategy
findings.headline: Retail investment properties make up 71% of 256-property portfolio while declining in value
findings.detail: Of the 256 properties held for investment, 183 are retail (valued at £148.419m), down from 187 properties the prior year. The total property portfolio value fell from £242.016m to £233.005m. With £88.995m of borrowing backing these assets, the portfolio carries material market risk.
findings.matters: Retail property values are under pressure from structural market shifts; a leveraged portfolio concentrated in this sector amplifies downside risk to the council's balance sheet and income stream.
findings.figures: Retail: 183 properties valued at £148.419m; Total portfolio: £233.005m; Borrowing backing commercial investments: £88.995m

findings.paper_title: Annex 6 - Capital and Investment Strategy
findings.headline: Borrowing jumps £17.3m while grant funding falls by £60.2m, shifting capital financing to debt dependency
findings.detail: Borrowing increases from £83.632m (2025/26) to £100.911m (2026/27), while grant funding collapses from £98.653m to £38.414m. Capital receipts remain minimal at £1.762m, leaving borrowing as the dominant financing mechanism for capital schemes.
findings.matters: This shift from grant-funded to borrowing-funded capital spending increases the council's debt service burden and signals either end of grant support or portfolio constraints.
findings.figures: Borrowing: £83.632m → £100.911m; Grants: £98.653m → £38.414m; Capital Receipts: £6.025m → £1.762m

findings.paper_title: Annex 6 - Capital and Investment Strategy
findings.headline: Housing company lending commitments escalating dramatically from £7.9m to £84.1m by 2028/29
findings.detail: The approved lending limit to the Council's Housing Company rises from £7.870m (2025/26 forecast) to £23.125m (2026/27), then £61.845m (2027/28) and £84.124m (2028/29). This represents a tenfold increase over three years, creating substantial ongoing debt service obligations.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's total debt commitments and whether these housing investments are generating sufficient returns to service the borrowing they support.

findings.paper_title: 12 Annual Governance Statement Update
findings.headline: DSG Deficit and Safety Valve Agreement outcome remains dependent on pending government policy
findings.detail: The council's DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) deficit under a Safety Valve Agreement was flagged as significant last year. While the paper reports 'positive progress' with the Department for Education and Treasury, the council is 'still awaiting a white paper from government on the long-term position,' introducing policy uncertainty.
findings.matters: The long-term financial liability of the DSG deficit and Safety Valve terms are material and contingent on government policy decisions beyond council control.
findings.figures: None provided in this paper
findings.quote: positive progress has been achieved during the year with the Department for Education and Treasury in unlocking further progress in this area. A further verbal update can be given at the meeting as we are still awaiting a white paper from government on the long-term position regarding this national risk area.

findings.paper_title: 12 Annual Governance Statement Update
findings.headline: Children's Services identified as the primary driver of financial pressure
findings.detail: The paper explicitly names Children's Services as the key financial pressure. The council notes that 'significant attention and oversight at Officer and Member level continues,' suggesting this is a structural issue without clear resolution path.
findings.matters: Children's Services overspends are typically structural and persistent; identifying it as the single key pressure indicates limited near-term budget stabilisation.
findings.figures: None provided in this paper
findings.quote: The key pressure remains in Children's Services and significant attention and oversight at Officer and Member level continues.

findings.paper_title: 12 Annual Governance Statement Update
findings.headline: Council projecting year-end overspend despite improved financial position
findings.detail: The council's financial position has improved compared to 2024/25 but it continues to project an overspend when accounts close. The paper does not provide specific figures, only that the position is 'whilst still difficult' and that Fair Funding reforms have compounded the challenge.
findings.matters: Persistent year-end overspends indicate expenditure control challenges and constrained financial flexibility, relevant to debt capacity assessment.
findings.figures: None provided in this paper
findings.quote: However, our financial position whilst still difficult has improved since last year but we are still projecting an overspend as at the end of the year.

findings.paper_title: E3661 - 2026-27 Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: The council explicitly states that uncertainty in this strategy is 'abnormally high' due to Fair Funding uncertainties
findings.detail: The council identifies abnormally elevated risk in its financial forecasting, driven by uncertainty around Fair Funding implementation. At the time of writing, the government had not published final Fair Funding results. The council states: 'The level of uncertainty and risk is abnormally high for this strategy due to the uncertainties and impacts of Fair Funding which have compounded an already challenging financial position.'
findings.matters: When a council describes its own financial forecasting as abnormally uncertain, it signals that projected figures may change materially and that planning for recovery is difficult. This heightens lending risk.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The level of uncertainty and risk is abnormally high for this strategy due to the uncertainties and impacts of Fair Funding

findings.paper_title: E3661 - 2026-27 Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Government's Fair Funding grant reforms are forecast to have a 'significant negative impact' on the council's financial position
findings.detail: Fair Funding—a new government mechanism for allocating grants via a revised funding formula—is identified as a primary driver of the council's financial stress. The council explicitly states it 'will have a significant negative impact on the Council's financial position' and notes this has 'compounded an already challenging financial position.' At the time of writing, the government had not published final implementation details, forcing the strategy to model 'initial government proposals.'
findings.matters: Fair Funding represents a structural, externally-driven threat to revenues that is outside the council's control and will persist through the medium term.
findings.figures: Impact not quantified separately; modelled as part of the £9.87m gap
findings.quote: that it will have a significant negative impact on the Council's financial position

findings.paper_title: E3661 - 2026-27 Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.headline: Bath & North East Somerset faces an £8.9m budget gap for 2026/27 that remains unfunded even after identified savings proposals
findings.detail: The MTFS identifies an annual funding gap of £9.87m for 2026/27. Council savings proposals total only £0.96m, leaving a remaining funding gap of £8.91m (95% of the initial gap). The problem is multi-year: the council projects funding gaps of £10.06m (2027/28), £9.90m (2028/29), £4.94m (2029/30), and £4.82m (2030/31), totalling £38.63m over five years.
findings.matters: An unfunded gap this large—with identified solutions covering less than 10% of the shortfall—indicates a structural financial problem and severely constrained financial capacity.
findings.figures: Budget gap £8.9m, savings proposals £0.96m, remaining gap £8.91m, total five-year shortfall £38.63m
findings.quote: the current MTFS shows a budget gap of £8.9m for 2026/27

findings.paper_title: 10a External Audit Annual Audit Report Appendix 1
findings.headline: Planned staff survey did not take place in 2024 due to restructuring, limiting evidence of control effectiveness.
findings.detail: The Council did not undertake a planned staff survey in 2024 due to restructuring work, though it plans to do so in 2025. This reduced in-year assurances available to audit over the effectiveness of governance and control arrangements.
findings.matters: Staff surveys provide early warning of control and governance breakdowns. Postponement due to restructuring signals organizational disruption affecting normal governance processes.
findings.figures: Planned staff survey postponed from 2024 to 2025; standards committee did not meet in public during year
findings.quote: The Council did not undertake a staff survey as planned in 2024 due to restructuring work - but plans to undertake this in 2025.

findings.paper_title: 10a External Audit Annual Audit Report Appendix 1
findings.headline: Cultural assets and parking income significantly underperformed in 2024/25, creating identified income risks in the medium-term plan.
findings.detail: The Council identified income risks from cultural assets and parking in its medium-term financial strategy. These underperformed in 2024/25. With MTFS identifying a £15.3m funding gap over the next five years, income volatility creates a risk to balanced budgets.
findings.matters: Income-dependent budgets are less controllable than expenditure. Underperforming income lines in a council facing £15m five-year funding gaps indicate structural revenue problems.
findings.figures: Identified income risks from cultural assets and parking; MTFS funding gap £15.3m; planned savings £13.3m
findings.quote: Financial planning includes income risks from cultural assets and parking, which underperformed in 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: 10a External Audit Annual Audit Report Appendix 1
findings.headline: Capital programme profiling remains weak; only 75% delivery with £16.2m rephased, and DfE has questioned plan feasibility due to delays.
findings.detail: Capital expenditure delivered £53.0m against a £70.5m budget (75%), with £16.2m rephased into future years. More concerning, the DfE provided feedback stating the Council's DSG recovery plan requires revision due to delays in the capital programme, given reliance on capital sufficiency work. This suggests delivery confidence is deteriorating.
findings.matters: Weak capital programme delivery undermines credibility with government stakeholders and impacts the critical DSG recovery plan. Capital-funded school places (part of DSG solution) may not materialize as promised.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure £53.0m against budget £70.5m (75% delivery); rephased £16.2m
findings.quote: Capital expenditure was £53.0m against a £70.5m budget (75% delivery), with £16.2m rephased... The DfE has provided feedback, however, indicating that the Council's plans required revision and further evidence of the impact of mitigating actions, due to delays in the Council's capital programme.

findings.paper_title: 10a External Audit Annual Audit Report Appendix 1
findings.headline: Children's Services posted £6.2m overspend despite overall small revenue budget surplus, masking service-level pressure.
findings.detail: Children's Services overspent by £6.2m in 2024/25, offset only by a £5.3m underspend in Corporate budgets to produce a reported £0.21m revenue overspend overall. This single-service overspend of this scale indicates consistent demand and cost pressures in a statutory service area.
findings.matters: Demand-driven overspends in statutory services (children, SEND) are the hardest to control through savings and represent structural budget stress. The offset from corporate budgets may not be sustainable.
findings.figures: Children's Services overspend £6.2m; Corporate underspend £5.3m; net revenue overspend £0.21m
findings.quote: While there were significant variances across portfolios, Children's Services overspent by £6.2m, offset by a £5.3m underspend in Corporate budgets.

findings.paper_title: 10a External Audit Annual Audit Report Appendix 1
findings.headline: Savings delivery consistently short: only 77% of target delivered in 2024/25 with £0.98m delayed to following year.
findings.detail: The Council's 2024/25 savings target was £16.4m. Of this, £12.7m (77%) was delivered in full, £2.78m was mitigated by other means, and £0.98m slipped to 2025/26. Auditors retain a prior-year recommendation that the Council develop a single transformation plan to improve governance and delivery. The Council has committed to combining all transformation activities into one plan by 2025/26.
findings.matters: Repeated failure to deliver full savings targets forces reliance on contingency reserves and other offsetting underspends, reducing financial flexibility. The DSG crisis and capital programme delays indicate structural delivery problems beyond just savings.
findings.figures: 2024/25 savings target £16.4m; delivered in full £12.7m (77%); mitigated £2.78m; delayed £0.98m
findings.quote: In 2024/25 the savings target was £16.4m, of which £12.7m (77%) was delivered in full, £2.78m was mitigated by other means and the remaining £0.98m was delayed until 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 10a External Audit Annual Audit Report Appendix 1
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has grown £10.5m to £32.8m and the Council remains outside its Safety Valve recovery plan with no DfE funding received.
findings.detail: The cumulative DSG deficit rose to £32.8m by March 2025. The Council was suspended from its Safety Valve programme in 2024 after failing to deliver required savings, and received no Safety Valve payments in 2024/25. DfE feedback indicates the Council's revised plan still requires further evidence of impact. The forecast deficit will reach £65.8m by end of 2027/28 when the statutory override ends, with annual financing costs around £1.6m.
findings.matters: This is identified as a significant weakness by the auditors (key recommendation). While currently covered by reserves at £91.8m, the projected £65.8m shortfall poses serious refinancing risk if government policy requires deficit recovery after 2027/28, and the £1.6m annual financing cost represents ongoing drain on cash flow.
findings.figures: DSG deficit £32.8m (up £10.5m); forecast deficit £65.8m by end 2027/28; annual financing cost c£1.6m; general fund reserves £91.8m
findings.quote: The Council remains outside its agreed Safety Valve (SV) plan, and no SV payments were received in 2024/25... The forecast cumulative deficit at the end of 2027/28 - when the statutory override now ends following the recent two-year extension - is £65.8m.

findings.paper_title: 9c Audit Findings Report Council Pension Fund Appendix 3
findings.headline: Commercial Estate generating £0.5m adverse variance; surplus properties consuming resources with planned maintenance savings target not being met
findings.detail: The council's Corporate Estate ended the year £0.5m over budget due to high running costs of surplus properties and loss of income from un-let buildings. The council acknowledges this means 'an ongoing savings target to reduce maintenance costs across the estate is not being met'.
findings.matters: The council's property rationalisation programme is not delivering planned savings; surplus space is a drag on finances with no clear exit strategy, suggesting poor property portfolio management
findings.figures: £0.5m adverse variance in Corporate Estate
findings.quote: The Corporate Estate ended the year with an adverse budget position of £0.5m, resulting from high running costs of surplus properties and loss of income from un-let buildings, which in turn means an ongoing savings target to reduce maintenance costs across the estate is not being met.

findings.paper_title: 9c Audit Findings Report Council Pension Fund Appendix 3
findings.headline: Investment Property portfolio declined £9.012m in value during 2024/25; council property investment strategy underperforming
findings.detail: The council's Investment Property asset class fell by £9.012m since the last full valuation in March 2024, representing a significant unrealised loss on commercial real estate holdings.
findings.matters: Council's property investment returns are negative; suggests broader commercial real estate market weakness and indicates the council's property holdings strategy may not be delivering the income generation the budget depends on
findings.figures: £9.012m reduction in Investment Property asset values
findings.quote: A £9.012m reduction in Investment Property values has occurred since the last full valuation was undertaken (31st March 2024)

findings.paper_title: 9c Audit Findings Report Council Pension Fund Appendix 3
findings.headline: Collection Fund performance deteriorated by £1.460m versus estimate; Business Rates declining due to Empty Property and Retail Relief increases
findings.detail: The council estimated a Collection Fund surplus of £6.925m but achieved only £5.465m. The shortfall is driven by increased Empty Property Relief and Retail Relief reducing Business Rates income, signalling local economic stress in the commercial property market.
findings.matters: Business Rates are volatile and council-dependent; increasing relief claims suggest local businesses are struggling, which will affect future income and may presage further economic deterioration in the area
findings.figures: Estimated £6.925m surplus; actual £5.465m; variance £1.460m adverse
findings.quote: At an overall level, the outturn position on the Collection Fund position worsened by £1.460m over the estimated position. The main reason for the surplus reduction relating to Business Rates is due to an increase in Empty Property Relief and Retail Relief, partially offset by improved Bad Debt provision.

findings.paper_title: 9c Audit Findings Report Council Pension Fund Appendix 3
findings.headline: National Insurance funding shortfall of £1.3m in 2025/26; government grant covers only 50% of the council's employer NI cost increase
findings.detail: The council's direct staffing cost increase from employers National Insurance is £2.6m in 2025/26. The government's allocation methodology leaves a £1.3m gap that the council must absorb from its own budget.
findings.matters: This is a structural cost pressure that will recur annually; it indicates that government has not fully compensated councils for cost changes, and the council must find offsetting savings elsewhere
findings.figures: £2.6m total NI cost increase; £1.3m unfunded shortfall (50% gap)
findings.quote: The final grant allocation creates a £1.3m shortfall in funding of the Council's direct staffing cost increase of £2.6m from the Employers National Insurance increases in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 9c Audit Findings Report Council Pension Fund Appendix 3
findings.headline: Revenue support grant collapsed from £31m (2013/14) to £1.3m (2025/26), forcing structural dependence on volatile local taxation and commercial income
findings.detail: Over 12 years the council's central government support has been reduced by 96%. The council explicitly states it has become 'more reliant on external income to help fund core Council services', meaning local services now depend on Council Tax, Business Rates and commercial revenues rather than protected grant funding.
findings.matters: This fundamental structural shift makes the council far more exposed to local economic volatility, Council Tax base changes, and commercial income pressures; it indicates the council is no longer supported by central government for baseline service delivery
findings.figures: £31m in 2013/14 declining to £1.3m in 2025/26 (95.8% reduction)
findings.quote: The Council revenue support grant has reduced from £31m in 2013/14 to £1.3m per annum in 2025/26 and as a result we have become more reliant on external income to help fund core Council services.

findings.paper_title: 9c Audit Findings Report Council Pension Fund Appendix 3
findings.headline: Future years budget gap deferred from 2026/27 onwards; recovery dependent on income growth and efficiencies not yet secured
findings.detail: The council balanced the 2025/26 budget but acknowledges 'a future years budget gap from 2026/27, although this is expected to reduce to a balanced position once the impacts of income growth and further efficiencies are factored in'. This defers the problem rather than solving it.
findings.matters: Medium-term financial sustainability is uncertain; the council is betting on future income growth and cost reductions that are not yet locked in, suggesting the structural budget gap remains unresolved
findings.figures: Budget gap deferred to 2026/27 onwards; £14.01m funding gap closed for 2025/26 only through £6.70m income generation + £7.31m savings
findings.quote: The updated plan shows a balanced budget for 2025/26 with a future years budget gap from 2026/27, although this is expected to reduce to a balanced position once the impacts of income growth and further efficiencies are factored in to budget planning.

findings.paper_title: 9c Audit Findings Report Council Pension Fund Appendix 3
findings.headline: Children's Services £6.179m overspend in 2024/25 driven by £3.37m residential placement pressure from safeguarding needs and mental health crisis
findings.detail: Core statutory children's services overspent by £6.179m. The largest pressure is residential placements (£3.37m over budget) attributable to criminal exploitation, emotional dysregulation and mental health issues. Disabled Children's Team £1.28m over, UASC £0.37m over, Home to School Transport £1.40m over from driver shortages and cost inflation.
findings.matters: These are non-discretionary statutory services protecting vulnerable children; the fact that safeguarding demand for criminal exploitation victims is driving major overspends indicates a structural social problem the council cannot control, and the combined pressures suggest savings plans targeting children's services will be difficult to achieve
findings.figures: £6.179m total overspend; £3.37m residential placements; £1.28m Disabled Children's Team; £1.40m Home to School Transport
findings.quote: The biggest area of demand-led pressure is Residential (£3.37m over budget), this has been driven by an increase in numbers of placements because of the need to safeguard young people suffering criminal exploitation, in addition to an increased trend of young people suffering from emotional dysregulation and mental health, in conjunction with upward cost pressures on placements from providers.

findings.paper_title: 9c Audit Findings Report Council Pension Fund Appendix 3
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant accumulated deficit of £32.795m with Safety Valve recovery plan funding being reprofiled
findings.detail: The council carries a DSG overspend of £10.532m in 2024/25 combined with an accumulated deficit of £22.263m (total £32.795m). Under a Safety Valve Agreement with the DFE since March 2023, only £8.23m has been received to date, with remaining payments being reprofiled pending agreement of a revised recovery plan.
findings.matters: This is the largest contingent liability on the council's balance sheet and creates a structural funding dependency on continued DFE support; if the reprofiled payments do not materialise or if the plan is rejected, the council cannot fund this from its general fund reserves
findings.figures: £32.795m total (£22.263m accumulated + £10.532m current year overspend); £8.23m received to date of Safety Valve funding
findings.quote: The centrally held elements of the DSG were over budget by £10.532m, due to significant increases in numbers and cost of placements for children with SEND, which is funded from the High Needs Block within the DSG. This overspend will be carried forward along with the accumulated deficit on the DSG of £22.263m giving a total overspend to be carried forward of £32.795m.

findings.paper_title: 9a Audit Findings Report Council Pension Fund Appendix 1
findings.headline: Senior officer remuneration disclosure contained errors including £17,522 pension cost variance
findings.detail: Testing of senior officer remuneration found that one interim staff member's role was not disclosed, and one senior manager's pension contribution was disclosed as £5,653 when it should have been £23,175 — a variance of £17,522 above performance materiality for this disclosure (which has a lower materiality threshold of £20k).
findings.matters: Errors in senior officer pay disclosures undermine transparency and suggest weak control over a sensitive disclosure area where public interest is high.
findings.figures: £17,522 pension cost error; materiality for this disclosure is £20k
findings.quote: Agreement of salaries and pension costs for the year identified an error in the pension contribution for one senior manager. This had been disclosed as £5,653 whereas the actual figure is £23,175. This is a variance of £17,522

findings.paper_title: 9a Audit Findings Report Council Pension Fund Appendix 1
findings.headline: £470k depreciation charge omitted for asset that became operational in year
findings.detail: An asset that became operational during the financial year was not depreciated in accordance with the council's accounting policy. This resulted in a £470k understatement in the depreciation charge that was not corrected.
findings.matters: Non-depreciation of operational assets indicates either a control gap in the asset lifecycle process or weak compliance with accounting policies, both of which raise governance concerns.
findings.figures: £470k depreciation charge omitted
findings.quote: We identified one asset, which had become operational in year, had not been depreciated, in line with the Authority's accounting policies and, therefore, a charge of £470k for the year should have been incurred

findings.paper_title: 9a Audit Findings Report Council Pension Fund Appendix 1
findings.headline: Pension fund net liability of £52.881m; audit certificate cannot be issued until pension fund auditor letter received
findings.detail: The council's pension liability fell significantly from £92.413m to £52.881m. The auditor cannot complete the 2024-25 audit certificate due to awaiting the letter of assurance from the Avon Pension Fund auditor, plus an outstanding objection from the 2023-24 audit.
findings.matters: A £52.8m pension liability is material to the council's balance sheet. The fact the audit certificate cannot be issued is unusual and signals unresolved issues or technical complications with the pension fund audit.
findings.figures: £52.881m net pension liability (down from £92.413m in prior year)
findings.quote: We intend to delay the certification of the closure of the 2024/25 audit of Bath and North East Somerset Council in the audit report, due to the 2023-24 audit certificate remaining open as a result of an objection to the final statements being received and considered

findings.paper_title: 9a Audit Findings Report Council Pension Fund Appendix 1
findings.headline: Multiple IT control deficiencies including user access issues and unremediaged cybersecurity policy gaps
findings.detail: The auditor identified that outdated cybersecurity policies (acceptable use last reviewed Sept 2023, data retention marked draft). Seven IT staff have duplicate privileged accounts with administrator rights. Access control requests can be made via personal assistants rather than through formal channels. The council was in transition on these issues but gaps remain.
findings.matters: IT control weaknesses increase the risk of fraud, data breach, or system compromise. For a council managing major property assets and receiving public funds, cyber risk is material.
findings.figures: 7 IT staff with duplicate admin accounts
findings.quote: From our IT audit review we note that the Authority has not updated the following policies in a timely manner (bracket shows due date for review). – Acceptable use policy (Sept 2023)

findings.paper_title: 9a Audit Findings Report Council Pension Fund Appendix 1
findings.headline: No formal approval process for journals under £500k; management can post their own transactions
findings.detail: The auditor notes that finance team members can post their own journals below £500k with no formal approval. The auditor identified that one user with admin access should not have had journal posting ability. There is also no audit trail documenting review of capital journals above £500k despite management saying they review them.
findings.matters: Lack of segregation of duties in the general ledger is a fundamental control weakness that increases fraud risk and weakens financial statement reliability.
findings.figures: Threshold of £500k; 7 IT staff have duplicate admin accounts
findings.quote: As in previous years we note that no formal approval process exists for those journals under £500k and assurance is taken from review of a sample of journals, below this threshold, on a monthly basis.

findings.paper_title: 9a Audit Findings Report Council Pension Fund Appendix 1
findings.headline: £3.124m in audit adjustments to financial statements, mostly from property valuation errors
findings.detail: The auditor identified multiple errors in property valuations. An investment property was overstated by £1.862m due to incorrect calculation. Land and buildings were initially understated by £4.418m until the valuer's report was received late. Investment properties were understated by £568k. These adjustments had no impact on usable reserves.
findings.matters: Material valuation errors in a council's largest asset category (properties totalling £563m) indicate either weak valuation processes or late delivery of external valuations, both governance concerns.
findings.figures: £3.124m total adjustment: investment property +£1.862m, land and buildings -£4.418m, investment property -£568k
findings.quote: We have identified 2 adjustments to the financial statements that have resulted in a £3.2m adjustment to the Authority's Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement.

findings.paper_title: 9a Audit Findings Report Council Pension Fund Appendix 1
findings.headline: Auditor identifies significant weakness in value-for-money arrangements, specifically around Dedicated Schools Grant deficit management
findings.detail: The auditor has concluded that the council has not made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources. One specific significant weakness identified relates to the council's arrangements for managing an ongoing Dedicated Schools Grant deficit, indicating the council may be struggling to control spending in a material service area.
findings.matters: VFM concerns signal that a council is not managing its finances efficiently and may face future financial distress, which directly affects borrowing risk.
findings.figures: Not quantified in the report headline
findings.quote: We identified a significant weakness(s) in the Authority's arrangements and so are not satisfied that the Authority has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources.

news_drafts.headline: Capital Financing Requirement of £386m substantially exceeds borrowing of £289m, with £97m gap filled by reserve drawdown
news_drafts.lead: Using reserves to fund capital rather than borrowing erodes the council's reserves and flexibility. Once reserves are exhausted, the council will need to borrow further or defer capital spending.

news_drafts.headline: Pension contribution prepayment consumed £20m of annual new borrowing
news_drafts.lead: Pension prepayment decisions indicate forward cash planning but also represent a committed outflow that reduces borrowing capacity available for other capital or service needs.

news_drafts.headline: Capital programme rephasing reduced debt repayment charges in the year
news_drafts.lead: Capital programme delays indicate delivery risk and suggest planned capital spending may not materialise, which affects medium-term financial planning and service infrastructure investment.
